    <title>Self-prediction residuals improve single-pass detection of wrong-object boxes in grounded vision-language models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:42:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28632v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28632v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Grounded vision-language models write boxes as text, and the mean probability of their coordinate tokens says little about whether a box is right. We study a single-pass signal for boxes on another object, which matter when only the object counts. A linear map, fitted per model to its own answers without labels, reads a box from the hidden state before writing. Its disagreement with the written box, the self-prediction residual, flags boxes on another object although the read-out is far less accurate; the residual's weight was fixed with labels on two models. On a replication list of 1,200 RefCOCOg test items, the residual, averaged over six models, raises the detection of these errors for each of fifteen single-pass scores, by 0.026 to 0.049 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) on a label-free probe and probes trained on 2,000 labelled items. Over all errors, adding it to the label-free probe moves AUROC, averaged over the models, by less than 0.02 (95% interval). With a fifth of answers reviewed, the share of all errors caught moves from 0.518 to 0.524, that of boxes on another object from 0.505 to 0.607 (post hoc): the residual changes which errors are found, not how many, and in cost-weighted recall it breaks even when such a box costs about 0.86 times another error, and its gain is positive in point estimate at equal costs. These gains come from RefCOCOg lists of MS-COCO images.</summary>

    <title>Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:31:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28628v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28628v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.</summary>

    <title>A High-Frequency Flux-Driven DC-SQUID Threshold Detector at the Single-Microwave-Photon Energy Scale: A Numerical Feasibility Study</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:24:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28627v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28627v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In our recent work (Phys. Rev. B \textbf{113}, 224503 (2026)), we showed numerically that rapidly sweeping the bias current of a current-biased Josephson junction threshold detector (CBJJ-JTD) drives it out of equilibrium. This substantially reduces the effect of thermal noise on microwave detection and may enable threshold detection near the energy of a single microwave photon. The scheme requires very low damping ($β\leq 10^{-4}$) and a very fast bias-current sweep ($v/β\geq 1$), both of which are difficult to achieve with available junctions and low-pass-filtered cryogenic measurement lines. Here we propose a more experimentally accessible nonequilibrium threshold detector based on a high-frequency flux-driven direct-current superconducting quantum interference device (DC-SQUID) and investigate it by numerically solving the resistively and capacitively shunted junction (RCSJ) equations. The applied flux drives a circulating supercurrent and sustains nonequilibrium phase dynamics throughout the bias-current sweep, removing the need for a fast sweep or for transient oscillations set by the initial phase. Using typical experimental device parameters, we calculate switching-current distributions (SCDs) with and without a microwave input for both driven and undriven SQUIDs. We quantify detection performance using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and their area under the curve (AUC). The simulations show that high-frequency flux drive reduces the impact of thermal noise and enables statistical discrimination of weak microwave pulses at the single-photon energy scale. We also numerically estimate detector characteristics such as phase selectivity and dynamic range.</summary>

    <title>Neural Schrödinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:17:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28623v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28623v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.</summary>

    <title>Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:16:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28621v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28621v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation. Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/yamanoko/dao/tree/main}{here}.</summary>

    <title>Distilling Visual Agents from Limited Interaction Experience</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:09:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28618v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28618v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.</summary>

    <title>VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:09:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28617v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28617v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.</summary>

    <title>Fast World Planner: Advantage-Aware Action-Chunk Policy for Online Planning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:04:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28616v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28616v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28615v1</id>
    <title>Can Ideologues Agree on Quality? From Non-identifiable Latent Factors to Collective Outcomes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T06:59:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28615v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28615v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>To surface "objective" fact-check notes, X's Community Notes uses Biased Matrix Factorization (BMF) on crowd-sourced ratings to separate note quality from reviewer ideology. We show that for any correctly specified model that decomposes ratings into quality and ideological alignment, this separation requires fixing an ideological anchor: a reference point for what counts as neutral. We give a characterization for the standard implementation: with $L_2$ regularization, BMF anchors quality at a point proportional to the mean reviewer ideology, recovering objective quality if and only if the mean reviewer is neutral, assuming note quality is uncorrelated with note leaning. This parallels the Condorcet Jury Theorem: collective judgment recovers truth when the pool is unbiased on average. When that assumption fails, BMF's recovered ranking shifts toward maximizing aggregate reviewer satisfaction, which coincides with social welfare only when the pool is representative. This is not specific to BMF; the rating matrix admits a continuous family of gauge-equivalent decompositions, each implying a different quality ranking, so no mechanism based on ratings alone can recover quality without implicitly choosing such an anchor. What appears to be routine hyperparameter tuning is in fact a normative choice about whose preferences define quality.</summary>

    <title>Internalized Experience: How Training Data Shapes Memory Formation in LLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T06:54:36Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28613v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28613v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Parametric memory enables large language models (LLMs) to retain information from past experience and reuse it in subsequent tasks. Yet how training data supports the internalization of reusable task rules remains unclear. We introduce FSMem (Finite-State Machine Memory), a state-transition framework for constructing training data and studying how data content and organization shape memory formation. We evaluate rule reuse across synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution through valid-action identification and execution-outcome prediction, complemented by next-operation prediction in code. Our experiments reveal several systematic learning patterns. Under matched training conditions, even unchanged task rules become harder to internalize when learned alongside a larger variety of action types; by contrast, scaling the training data to provide broader state-action coverage generally improves rule learning. We further find that training at a single execution depth produces depth-specialized behavior, with models performing best when training and test executions have similar lengths. Motivated by this finding, we construct cumulative corpora that combine short and long trajectories, which can outperform long-trajectory-only training while using fewer training tokens. Together, these results demonstrate that the same task rules can be internalized differently depending on how execution experience is constructed, and that understanding these learning patterns can guide the design of more effective training data for parametric memory.</summary>

    <title>Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T06:47:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28611v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28611v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reinforcement-learning agents shape the observations they encounter; consequently, detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) states requires analysing action-conditioned trajectories rather than treating inputs as independent samples. We propose Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility (ACTI), a detector that evaluates forward and backward transition likelihoods, calibrates this comparison against the in-distribution profile at each timestep, and smooths the score over a short window, using no future information. We tested ACTI across six environments and fifteen detectors within OOD-RL-Bench, using the four anomaly mechanisms that qualified in every environment, with ten policy replicates per environment. All primary metrics are matched-time: each score after anomaly onset is compared with a clean twin rollout's score at the same timestep. Our method secured the top macro matched-time AUROC, outperforming the dynamics-model baseline (PEDM), while scoring transitions roughly two orders of magnitude faster. Compared to the state-only variant, ACTI achieved a small but consistent AUROC gain and a shorter detection delay. The capacity-matched forward-only baseline, ACTI-Forward, secured a statistically significant advantage in AUPRC alongside a reduced detection delay. The discrepancy in AUROC did not reach statistical significance. Ablation studies suggest instead that performance improvements stem from action conditioning, calibration at each timestep, and smoothing of the transition-likelihood scores. Based on these results, we recommend using ACTI-Forward.</summary>

    <title>Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T06:43:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28610v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28610v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.</summary>

    <title>BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T06:36:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28607v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28607v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.</summary>

    <title>Bridging Teacher-Student Capability Gaps with Recurrent Computation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T06:28:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28603v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.</summary>

    <title>DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T06:01:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28595v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.</summary>

    <title>MedCoast: Semantic Abstraction of Reasoning Trajectories for Test-Time Biomedical Question Answering</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:38:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28586v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28586v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. While test-time search methods such as Tree-of-Thought can improve reasoning performance, directly searching over free-form language is computationally expensive and highly redundant, as many reasoning trajectories contain semantically equivalent intermediate steps expressed in different surface forms. We introduce MedCoast, an offline-to-online reasoning framework that converts sampled chain-of-thought trajectories into a compact space for structured process supervision. Offline, we recursively cluster semantically similar reasoning steps under shared prefixes to construct an abstract reasoning tree that captures recurring clinical reasoning patterns. We then derive node-level supervision from progress toward correct solutions, and train a lightweight process reward model (PRM) to evaluate partial reasoning states. At inference time, the learned critic guides test-time exploration by prioritizing promising reasoning prefixes. Across seven biomedical QA benchmarks, MedCoast often improves over self-consistency under fixed inference budgets, with gains of up to 15 points. Despite using a reward model more than 50 times smaller, MedCoast achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art reward models in several settings, highlighting its potential for resource-constrained biomedical reasoning.</summary>

    <title>AsyncMixVLA: Runtime Asynchronous Robot Policy Switching for Adaptation to Dynamic Environments</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:37:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28585v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28585v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28584v1</id>
    <title>Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:36:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28584v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28584v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.</summary>

    <title>Understanding and Mitigating the Fragility of Self-Rewarding Optimization</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:27:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28582v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28582v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Self-rewarding optimization (SRO) promises to improve language models by enabling them to generate their own reward signals. Yet when and how SRO succeeds or fails remains poorly understood. We reveal that SRO is fundamentally fragile: even seemingly benign perturbations to training prompts can corrupt the self-generated preference signal and trigger iterative collapse. We demonstrate this through two prompt-level attacks that serve as controlled stress tests: a Re-Ranking attack that concentrates training on prompts where self-reward diverges from an oracle, and a Preamble attack that learns short prefixes inflating self-reward without any gain in oracle quality. To explain why these attacks succeed, we introduce self-reward fidelity (SRF), a metric quantifying on-policy agreement between self-evaluated and oracle rewards. We show that SRF can serve as a diagnostic signal of self-supervision reliability, and that controlled SRF perturbations induce a phase-transition region: SRO improves when SRF remains sufficiently high, but collapses once SRF drops below a model- and task-dependent threshold. This analysis motivates Projection Decoupling Defense, which suppresses SRO update components along directions to which the reward generator is locally sensitive, improving SRO robustness under adversarial conditions. This work sheds light on the fragility of SRO and charts promising directions toward making it more robust.</summary>

    <title>Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:23:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28579v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28579v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.</summary>

    <title>CLASP: Deciding Structure and Claims Before Decoding for Whole-Slide Pathology Report Generation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:16:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28576v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28576v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Whole-slide pathology report generation has advanced through stronger slide encoders, retrieved knowledge, and, recently, slide-level multimodal LLMs. However, these generators leave every report-level choice to the decoder: how long the report is, how it is organised, and which findings it states and where. On the standard PathText-BRCA benchmark, we find that these choices dominate n-gram overlap, as reports from the query's hospital selected without learning approach the state of the art, while decoders under-generate and fall back to the most frequent findings. We present CLASP, a decide-then-decode generator that makes these choices explicitly, once per slide. Before decoding, an Exemplar Structure Prior (ESP) takes the sentence plan and length from reports of image-similar cases, a Calibrated Claim Decision (CCD) selects the findings from calibrated slide posteriors, and a Claim-to-Sentence Placement (CSP) assigns each finding to a planned sentence. A Plan-Conditioned Decoder (PCD), refined by structure-anchored sequence training, then writes the report under these decisions. With 35M parameters, CLASP outperforms retrained report generators and slide-level LLMs of up to 7B parameters, matches the strongest published results, and generalises to lung cancer from unseen hospitals. Its decisions change what the reports state, not only their length, transfer to an LLM decoder, and can withhold what H&E cannot show: withholding receptor status leaves 23% fewer contradictions with clinical records than the same network without decisions.</summary>

    <title>EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:14:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28574v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28574v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.</summary>

    <title>MACE: Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation of Frozen Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:13:05Z</updated>

    <summary>In plant phenotyping, crop disease diagnosis has traditionally relied on expert assessment of visible symptoms and on models tailored to specific crops or diseases, and both are difficult to scale across field conditions. Recent methods provide frozen vision-language models with source-grounded knowledge bases that summarize the typical symptoms of each disease but describe little of how symptoms vary across individual cases. We introduce MACE (Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation), a training-free method that supplements the knowledge base with a memory of symptom descriptions paired with known disease labels. MACE matches a description of the query image against this memory and retrieves only text descriptions and disease labels, so the query is the only image that the diagnosis model sees. Across ten crops, MACE with Claude Sonnet 5.5 improved accuracy over the knowledge-base baseline from 42.8% to 62.2% in distribution and from 50.7% to 57.0% on held-out image collections.     <title>Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:12:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28572v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28572v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|ψ|^2$, yet it is $ψ$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover $|ψ|^2$ directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates $ψ$ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast $2ρV/(1+ρ^2)$, and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, $2\mathrm{NA}/λ$, from the photons alone.</summary>

    <summary>Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.</summary>

    <title>Beyond Unit Tests: Path-Aware Rubric-Guided LLM Autograding of Notebooks</title>

    <summary>Jupyter notebooks support open-ended, multi-step assessments in which students build one logical flow across interdependent steps, combining code, written analysis, and generated outputs such as plots. These reflect authentic scientific practice but are hard to grade consistently, since students may make different yet equally valid choices at each step, so a later answer can only be judged in light of the choices a student made earlier. We present an LLM-based autograder for such flow-structured notebook questions. It generates a rubric from a reference solution, then applies a softening pass that relaxes criteria tied to the reference so legitimate alternative paths are not penalized. Each question group is graded in a single model call, so later answers are judged against the student's own earlier choices, using question-type tags and schema-constrained, low-temperature outputs. Evidence is scored multimodally: code, text, numerical outputs, and figures from code cells. We deployed the tool in a machine-learning course, integrated with Gradescope, with a pre-submission format check and prompt-injection defenses, and evaluate it both in that live course and against archived submissions graded by staff in earlier terms. We report agreement, cross-model variance, cost, student perceptions, and injection resilience. With low-temperature models, agreement with human scores is often strong, including on the open-ended items the design specifically targets, while run-to-run stability depends sharply on the model's temperature support.</summary>

    <summary>Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on external visual tools to access fine-grained visual evidence, but repeated tool execution incurs substantial inference overhead and deployment dependencies. Moreover, conventional tool-use RL can improve visual-task performance, yet the resulting tool gains are often unstable. Motivated by this, we propose Tool-to-Self (T2S), a tool-scaffolded reinforcement learning framework that turns external visual tools into temporary training scaffolds. T2S cold-starts tool-use ability and observation prediction from tool-repairable examples, then progressively anneals tool execution on a per-tool basis during RL. By combining answer-correctness and observation-consistency rewards with privileged on-policy self-distillation from actual tool observations, T2S effectively teaches the model both to reproduce tool outputs and to reason from them. Experiments across diverse visual perception and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over both explicit tool-use models and implicit zooming models while enabling tool-free inference with reduced latency.</summary>

    <title>SAFE-DRIFT: Data Selection for Supervised Fine-tuning with Controllable Off-Target Drifts</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T04:26:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28560v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28560v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We propose SAFE-DRIFT, a data-selection framework for supervised fine-tuning that improves a target capability while controlling unwanted drift in the model's other behaviors. We formalize this as a constrained optimization problem that maximizes alignment with the target gradient, subject to a budget on off-target drift which we quantify using the Fisher information of a reference distribution. Under this objective, the optimal, closed-form update is a damped natural-gradient step that downweights reference-sensitive directions. To estimate these high-dimensional gradients and work within the right geometry, we further derive a scalable algorithm that approximates the Fisher information and the target gradient in a shared low-dimensional subspace and analyze how entanglement of the target and reference task can affect the update. We evaluate SAFE-DRIFT against state-of-the-art data selection methods across diverse domains including coding and medical question answering, yielding competitive target performance while reducing degradation on specified off-target behaviors.</summary>

    <title>From atomic events to material degradation across metre and year scales</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T04:26:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28559v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28559v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Material degradation emerges from microscopic events whose consequences accumulate over years, yet mechanism-resolved simulations remain confined below engineering timescales. The challenge is not just the sheer number of events: atomistic evolution is dominated by recurrent local motion, with only a tiny fraction driving lasting structural change. This distinction is not encoded in an instantaneous atomic configuration. Locally indistinguishable states can exhibit different event competition, escape times, and long-horizon outcomes, revealing missing kinetic context as a critical information bottleneck. This context spans space and time: the future consequence of a local transition depends on its surrounding defect environment and the kinetic history leading to its current state. To solve this, AtomWorld reconstructs a predictive kinetic state from multiscale structural observations and trajectory history, distinguishing transient fluctuations from microscopic pathways that drive persistent structural evolution. Learning operates only over transitions admitted by the underlying kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) process, preserving event legality, state evolution, and physical time. Across BCC Fe-Cu precipitation, FCC Ni-Cr-Al ordering, and HCP Zr-H interstitial transport, restoring kinetic context consistently advances persistent evolution while maintaining physical fidelity and transferring to unseen conditions. In irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steel, this approach achieves up to 420-fold greater persistent evolution under matched event budgets. Combined with scalable execution, it successfully extends mechanism-resolved trajectories to service-year timescales across metre-scale heterogeneous domains.</summary>

Blood (about 34 tablespoons) will be drawn 1 time. The blood will be frozen and stored in a laboratory at MD Anderson for future use to make the CTLs. If CMV comes back after your transplant, the blood will be used to create CTLs. To create CTLs, blood cells are grown in the laboratory and trained to kill CMV. If the blood is not used to make the CTLs within 3 years, it will be destroyed.

CTL Administration:

If your CMV becomes active after your stem cell transplant, you will receive the CTLs through a needle in your vein over 1-5 minutes one time, within 72 hours after CMV becomes active again. Before you receive the CTLs, you will receive Benadryl (diphenhydramine) and Tylenol (acetaminophen) by mouth to help reduce the risk of side effects. This can be done in either the hospital (if not yet discharged after your transplant) or in the outpatient clinic (if you are discharged).

Your vital signs will be monitored at the end of the infusion, and then at 30 and 60 minutes after the infusion. Your oxygen level will be measured by pulse oximetry. For this test, a clothespin-shaped clip will be placed on your finger for at least 30 minutes. If you are an outpatient, you will remain in the clinic for at least 1 hour after the CTL infusion.

If the CMV does not become active again after your stem cell transplant, you will not receive the CTL infusion.

Study Visits:

If the CMV does not become active again after your stem cell transplant, you will not receive the CTL infusion and your follow-up care will be done as per post-transplant standard of care.

If you receive the CTL infusion, you will have the tests/procedures listed below.

Within 48 hours before the CTL infusion:

* You will have a physical exam.
* Blood (about 6 tablespoons) will be drawn for routine tests and to check your kidney and liver function. Part of blood draw will be used for a pregnancy test for women who are able to become pregnant. To take part in this study, you must not be pregnant.

Once a week for 4 weeks, blood (about 4-8 tablespoons) will be drawn to check the level of CMV infection in your body. This may be done more often, if you doctor thinks it is needed.

About 1, 2, 3, and 4 weeks, and then about 3, 6, and 12 months after the CTL infusion:

* You will have a physical exam.
* Blood (about 4 tablespoons) will be drawn for routine tests and to check your kidney and liver function.

Blood (about 4 tablespoons) will be drawn for tests to learn more about the way the CTLs are working and how long they last in the body. This blood will be drawn before the CTL infusion, and then about 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months after the CTL infusion. If possible, the blood needed for these tests will be collected during blood draws for routine tests so that no additional needle sticks will be needed.

Follow-Up Visits:

Once a week for 6 weeks, and then about 3, 6, 9, and 12 months after the CTL infusion, you will be checked for signs of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) at every clinic visit. You were told about GVHD at the time of being prepared for transplant.

Length of Study:

Your participation on this study will end after your last follow-up visit about 12 months after the CTL infusion.

This is an investigational study. The use of CTLs to treat CMV infection is not FDA approved. At this time, CTLs are only being used to treat infections in research studies.

Up to 105 patients will take part in this study. To increase generalisation of the intervention the investigators intend to compare the PNNS advices (the French National Nutrition and Health Program) to a program targeted on the own capacities of each patient.","detailedDescription":"Long-term evolution of successful-treated older patients is not well-known except for survival. They seem more affected by physical than psychological problems. The combined effects of aging, cancer, and treatments on muscle function could have hindered their usual physical activity. Cancer is associated with frailty. Fried and coll have defined a frailty phenotype as a combination of 3 or more of 5 conditions: exhaustion, loss of weight, decreased muscle strength, slow gait speed and low physical activity. Frail subjects have a higher risk of physical or cognitive disability and death. An intervention able to prevent frailty is of great interest for the older cancer patient and their quality of life. An intervention consisting of phone-program in physical activity has been associated with a decrease in self-reported disability in five-year obese survivors from cancer.

Patients will be randomized in two arms (1:1 ratio). Arm 1: Physical activity advices according to a program adapted to physical status of the patient assessed using SPPB (short physical performance battery) and the IPAQ questionnaire. A monthly phone support during one year will be performed by an adapted physical activity instructor and delivery of PNNS guide for subjects older than 55 y old. Arm 2: Delivery of PNNS guide for subjects older than 55 year old: recommendation of 1/2 hour physical activity of any kind.

Each patient will be followed during 2 years: First visit (V1) will take place before treatment. The subsequent visits will take place at 3 months (V2), 6 months (V3), 1 year (V4), 18 months (V5) and 2 years (V6), in which patients will complete questionnaires (IPAQ, QLQ-C30, one day dietary intakes), have clinical examinations (weight, performance status/ ECOG) and will be tested for physical facilities (SPPB, micro-fet2). {"protocolSection":{"identificationModule":{"nctId":"NCT02368067","orgStudyIdInfo":{"id":"SERMC- Endometrial Carcinoma"},"organization":{"fullName":"Southeastern Regional Medical Center","class":"OTHER"},"briefTitle":"Improved Method of Detecting Cancer Metastases","officialTitle":"Study of Instillation Technique Using The Modified Intra- Uterine Manipulator Catheter With Methylene Blue, Isosulfan Blue or Indocyanine Green Dyes, Compared to Cervical Injection, For Sentinel Lymph Node Detection in Endometrial Carcinoma","acronym":"SITs"},"statusModule":{"statusVerifiedDate":"2015-02","overallStatus":"UNKNOWN","lastKnownStatus":"ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION","expandedAccessInfo":{"hasExpandedAccess":false},"startDateStruct":{"date":"2014-06"},"primaryCompletionDateStruct":{"date":"2015-06","type":"ESTIMATED"},"completionDateStruct":{"date":"2015-12","type":"ESTIMATED"},"studyFirstSubmitDate":"2014-11-17","studyFirstSubmitQcDate":"2015-02-13","studyFirstPostDateStruct":{"date":"2015-02-20","type":"ESTIMATED"},"lastUpdateSubmitDate":"2015-02-13","lastUpdatePostDateStruct":{"date":"2015-02-20","type":"ESTIMATED"}},"sponsorCollaboratorsModule":{"responsibleParty":{"type":"SPONSOR"},"leadSponsor":{"name":"Southeastern Regional Medical Center","class":"OTHER"}},"oversightModule":{"oversightHasDmc":false},"descriptionModule":{"briefSummary":"The purpose of this study is to compare the Instillation Technique Using The Modified Intra- Uterine Manipulator Catheter With Methylene Blue, Isosulfan Blue or Indocyanine Green Dyes, Compared to Cervical Injection, For Sentinel Lymph Node Detection in Endometrial Carcinoma.","detailedDescription":"Following consent, surgery will be determined by the physician thereby determining group assignment- i.e the laparoscopic surgery group oror the robotic assisted surgery group. Both groups will undergo SLN mapping by instillation and injection. The Laparotomy/Laparoscopy Group will have Lymphazurin by injection and instillation of methylene blue dye. The Robot Assisted Group will have ICG by injection and instillation of methylene blue. Patients will undergo total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingoophorectomy, pelvic and paraaortic lymphadenectomy through laparotomy, laparoscopic or robotic assisted surgery as clinically determined by their attending physician. Subjects will undergo this surgery whether or not enrolled in the study.

Any clinically indicated uterine manipulator will be acceptable. Potential subjects will be informed of the potential risks of this device so they may make an informed decision about participation in the study. However the manipulator is standard of care and is not a study related risk. Subjects who agree to this study procedure will be monitored for adverse events.

The dyes used in this study are commercially available and will be provided through internal funding from the CTCA Gynecology/Oncology Department. Potential subjects will be informed

of the potential risks of these drugs so they may make an informed decision about participation in the study. Subjects who agree to this study procedure will be monitored for adverse events.

After administration of anesthesia, the intra-uterine uterine manipulator catheter will be inserted using the following suggested instructions for use;

• After the standard of care vaginal prep with povidone-iodine or any other surgeon preference cleansing solution, expose the cervix using a vaginal speculum. No additional preparation of the cervix is needed.

Immediately following exposure pf the cervix with the speculum, and before introduction of the intra-uterine uterine manipulator with catheter, 4ml total of isosulfan 1% blue or ICG (depending on what route of surgery is being elected) dye will be delivered by cervical injection as follows:

* Using a 20 or 22 gauge spinal needle, inject dye into the cervix at the 12, 3, 6 and 9 o'clock positions.
* Each site will receive approximately 1ml of dye with ½ superficial just under the mucosa and the remainder approximately 1cm deep to the prior injection.

The 22 gauge needles are commercially available and will be provided as routine clinical care. Potential subjects will be informed of the potential risks of injection so they may make an informed decision about participation in the study. Subjects who agree to this study procedure will be monitored for adverse events.

• Introduce the uterine manipulator with catheter trans-cervically until the distal balloon is positioned in the lower portion of the uterus. This is no different from routine clinical care.

Immediately following cervical injection and placement of the uterine manipulator and once intra-abdominal, the first step in surgery will be to occlude both fallopian tubes, as typically done as part of this surgery, using electrocautery devices (e.g. Ligasure) for sealing only the tubes.

Immediately following occlusion of both fallopian tubes, the comparator instillation dye will be instilled into the uterine cavity through the pre-inserted intra-uterine uterine manipulator catheter as follows:

* Insert the clinically selected uterine manipulator as per standard clinical practice.
* Slowly inject the dye through the center uterine cavity catheter access port., Rapid injection of dye could cause high intrauterine pressure resulting in extravasation. Use slow constant pressure to instill the dye. This can be done by the surgical assistant or by the operating surgeon via a long extension tubing.

{"protocolSection":{"identificationModule":{"nctId":"NCT05112692","orgStudyIdInfo":{"id":"PPOS in ICSI for PCOS"},"organization":{"fullName":"Mansoura University","class":"OTHER"},"briefTitle":"Progestin-primed Ovarian Stimulation Protocol Versus GnRH Antagonist Protocol in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Patients Undergoing IVF/ICSI Cycles","officialTitle":"Progestin-primed Ovarian Stimulation Protocol Versus GnRH Antagonist Protocol in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Patients Undergoing IVF/ICSI Cycles"},"statusModule":{"statusVerifiedDate":"2021-10","overallStatus":"UNKNOWN","lastKnownStatus":"NOT_YET_RECRUITING","expandedAccessInfo":{"hasExpandedAccess":false},"startDateStruct":{"date":"2021-11","type":"ESTIMATED"},"primaryCompletionDateStruct":{"date":"2023-11","type":"ESTIMATED"},"completionDateStruct":{"date":"2023-12","type":"ESTIMATED"},"studyFirstSubmitDate":"2021-10-04","studyFirstSubmitQcDate":"2021-11-06","studyFirstPostDateStruct":{"date":"2021-11-09","type":"ACTUAL"},"lastUpdateSubmitDate":"2021-11-06","lastUpdatePostDateStruct":{"date":"2021-11-09","type":"ACTUAL"}},"sponsorCollaboratorsModule":{"responsibleParty":{"type":"SPONSOR"},"leadSponsor":{"name":"Mansoura University","class":"OTHER"}},"oversightModule":{"isFdaRegulatedDrug":false,"isFdaRegulatedDevice":false,"isUsExport":false},"descriptionModule":{"briefSummary":"The purpose of this trial is to compare the efficacy and safety of the PPOS protocol to the GnRH antagonist protocol in patients with PCOS who are undergoing IVF/ICSI cycles.","detailedDescription":"Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common metabolic dysfunction and heterogeneous endocrine disorder. It is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility, affecting approximately 10%-18% of reproductive age women worldwide.

It is usually characterized by a clustering of hyperandrogenism, hypersecretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and hyperinsulinaemia, which could result in the arrest of ovarian follicular growth, oligo-ovulation or anovulation, menstrual dysfunction, hirsutism, infertility, pregnancy and/or neonatal complications.

Women with PCOS undergoing IVF or Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) treatment because of infertility are increasing in number, and these patients have been well described, typically characterized by producing an increased number of oocytes but are often of poor quality leading to lower fertilization, implantation, and pregnancy rates and a higher miscarriage rate and incidence of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Increasing evidence raises the issue that impaired oocyte maturation and developmental competence in women with PCOS are possibly linked to abnormal endocrine/ paracrine factors, metabolic dysfunction and alterations in the intrafollicular microenvironment during folliculogenesis and follicle maturation.

Several clinical ovarian stimulation protocols have been used so far in women with PCOS undergoing IVF treatment to prevent a premature LH surge during controlled ovarian stimulation (COS); these primarily include gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist or antagonist protocols.

GnRH antagonists can competitively inhibit endogenous GnRH and produce an immediate and rapid decline in LH and Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels without the flare effect of a GnRH agonist, and their administration by subcutaneous injection in the late follicular phase prevents an LH surge.

With progress in embryo vitrification techniques, many studies have suggested that pregnancies that arise from the transfer of frozen-thawed IVF embryos appear to have better perinatal and pregnancy outcomes. Thus, GnRH antagonist regimens combined with a freeze-all strategy for women with PCOS are currently accepted as the most routine IVF procedures.

The progesterone's pituitary suppression was recently used in controlled ovarian stimulation and approved its efficacy in terms of low incidence of premature LH surge and comparable pregnancy outcomes to short protocols in infertile women of normal ovarian reserve and polycystic ovarian syndrome.

These data indicated that progestin treatment might improve oocyte quality compared with a GnRH antagonist during COS in these patients, plus there were the advantages of an oral administration route instead of repeated injections of GnRH antagonist, a lower drug price and more control over LH levels, which can reduce the patients' discomfort and costs.

Furthermore, to avoid a low response of the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis, a double trigger with GnRHa and a low dose of Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)(1000IU) was used to induce final oocyte maturation without increasing the risk of moderate or severe Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

Choosing the appropriate progestin is crucial to the success of the Progestin-primed ovarian stimulation protocol (PPOS). Previous studies have shown that both Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) and Utrogestan are effective oral alternatives for the PPOS protocol.

MPA is preferred over Utrogestan because the administration of a natural exogenous progesterone, such as Utrogestan, can interfere with serum progesterone measurement and lead to the neglect of possible premature luteinization. However, the use of MPA during ovarian stimulation may lead to stronger pituitary suppression and thus may require a higher dosage of gonadotrophin and a longer ovarian stimulation duration than that of the conventional ovarian stimulation protocol. Therefore, the investigators need to test more synthetic progestins to find the most suitable option for PPOS.

Dydrogesterone (DYG), which has a molecular structure similar to that of natural progesterone, is widely used for hormone replacement therapy, endometriosis treatment, menstrual disorders and luteal support in pregnancy and threatened miscarriage. However, unlike MPA, the use of DYG under the recommended dosage (10-20 mg) does not inhibit ovulation, and thus, the use of DYG as an alternative to MPA and as an appropriate progestin in the PPOS regimen has yet to be explored.

In this study, the investigators hypothesize that DYG can be used as an alternative progestin in the PPOS protocol. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is designed to investigate cycle characteristics and endocrinological profiles of patients taking gonadotrophin while using DYG co-treatment, and to compare pregnancy outcomes in first frozen embryo transfer (FET) cycles with GNRH antagonist protocol as a control."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) of Bilateral Ovaries"],"keywords":["Progestin","ICSI","antagonist"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["NA"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"PARALLEL","primaryPurpose":"TREATMENT","maskingInfo":{"masking":"QUADRUPLE","whoMasked":["PARTICIPANT","CARE_PROVIDER","INVESTIGATOR","OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR"]}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":200,"type":"ESTIMATED"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"PPOS group","type":"ACTIVE_COMPARATOR","description":"Patients will be coadministered with Human Menopausal Gonadotrophin (HMG) 150-225 international unit/day (IU/d) via intramuscular injection and oral DYG 20mg/d from menstrual cycle day 3 (MC3) to the day of triggering. The study assay is extra and experimental.","detailedDescription":"Overview of PD-1 inhibition for locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC Lung cancer (LC) is the most common malignancy-related death in the United States (causing deaths in \~ 86,380 men and \~71,660 women in 2015. Fifteen percent of LC patients present with Stage I disease, which is treated primarily with surgery, leading to a 5-year survival rate of 54%. Approximately 57% of LC patients are initially diagnosed with metastatic disease (Stage IV) with a corresponding 5-year survival rate of 4.2%.

More recently, major treatment responses have been observed with the use of immune checkpoint inhibitor proteins expressed on the surface of lymphocytes and other immune cells, most notably on cytotoxic T-cells. When bound to their specific ligand, often another surface-bound protein on a neighboring cell, they can transmit stimulatory or inhibitory signals to activate or inhibit the cellular adaptive immune response. Several studies showed that the predominant mechanism by which NSCLC evades detection and elimination by the immune system is by exploiting one such inhibitory pathway through the expression of programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1, B7-H1). PD-L1 then binds to its receptor, programmed cell death protein 1 (PD1), on surveilling lymphocytes and initiates a signaling cascade which leads to lymphocyte exhaustion, a state of impaired function. The most successful immune checkpoint inhibitors so far are anti PD1 or anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibodies that prevent PD1-PD-L1 interaction at the tumor-immune interface. In this pilot study, the investigators will investigate if Nilogen's functional ex vivo bioassay can predict therapeutic response to anti PD1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) or anti PD-L1 (atezolizumab) in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

Functional bioassay as a potential predictive biomarker. The intent of using anti-PD-1/PD-L1 as an anti-cancer therapeutic is to block one of the ways that tumors inhibit T cell function within the tumor microenvironment, allowing restoration of T cell function. Therefore, the investigators hypothesize that a bioassay that directly measures restoration of T cell function in the context of all of the elements of the tumor microenvironment could accurately predict whether or not a patient will be clinically responsive to a particular immunotherapeutic agent that is designed to target the tumor microenvironment. A tumor biopsy from a patient who will be clinically responsive to anti-PD-1 will contain inactive T cells that may have their functional activity restored by the provision of anti-PD-1/PD-L1 ex vivo, much like what is seen in the ex vivo experiments performed at Nilogen using the 3D-EX platform (www.nilogen.com). To assess tumor response to nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab the investigators will use their proprietary immune cell function analysis in tumor samples obtained by FNA biopsy upon treatment with nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab ex vivo.

Hypothesis

1. In 80% of patients, FNA samples will provide a sufficient number of viable tumor cells to perform ex vivo functional bioassays with nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab.
2. Patients whose tumor FNA samples fail to respond to nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab, in the 3D Ex-Vivo assays will likely not show a clinical response to systemic nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab treatment.

Study Objectives

Primary Objective To test whether it is feasible to perform the 3D-EX functional response bioassay in the context of patients with advanced NSCLC receiving treatment with nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab in a standard clinical setting.

Overall study design Eligible patients will have a histologic or cytologic diagnosis of NSCLC; advanced-stage disease who are appropriate candidates for therapy with nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab, and age greater than 18 years. Prior surgery, chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy are allowed. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are outlined in the appropriate section. All inclusion and exclusion criteria will be assessed within 6 weeks prior to the first dose of nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab. Baseline radiographic studies should be performed within 30 days of screening. This clinical study will require central IRB approval. Informed consent will be obtained from each patient prior to screening and enrolling in the study.

Nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab will be administered as per the established standard of care for the eligible population.

Prediction of Response to Nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab by Nilogen's 3D-EX Bioassay.

In previous preclinical and clinical studies the investigators showed that FNA samples provide a sufficient number of viable tumor cells to perform drug sensitivity assays ex-vivo. The assay protocol is optimized to process tumor FNA samples, where the tumor microenvironment is intact and contains tumor cells and all other tumor-infiltrating inflammatory cells as well as specialized tumor stroma. Prior to initiation of therapy, tumor samples will be collected by FNA from accessible tumor tissue. For the ex vivo assays, aspirates will be obtained from each patient after collection of biopsy samples required for SOC. The FNA samples will be immediately shipped to the Nilogen Laboratory. All proposed assays will be performed at the Nilogen Oncosystems laboratory in Tampa, FL according to CLIA standards.

Patients who do not have a site of disease that will provide enough tumor cells for analyses will be taken off study. In adequate samples, tumor FNA samples will be treated nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab at clinically relevant concentrations. At the end of incubation T-cell activation will be assessed by a proprietary approach including evaluation of drug-mediated changes in three parameters: (1) T-cell activation, (2) cytokine release and (3) gene expression profiles. The response rate to treatment will be scored for T-cell activity and correlated with patient outcome.

The investigators hypothesize that tumors that fail to respond ex vivo will not be likely to be responsive in vivo in cancer patients."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Non Small Cell Lung In order to be eligible for participation in this trial, the subject must:

1. Be willing and able to provide written informed consent for the trial.
2. Be at least 18 years of age on the day of signing informed consent.
3. Have a histologic or cytologic diagnosis of Stage IV NSCLC.
4. Must be medically eligible to receive nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab as the standard of care for the next line of therapy (must have previously received first line platinum doublet chemotherapy) as determined by their oncologist.
5. Have measurable disease based on RECIST 1.1 (see section 7.1 or appropriate number).
6. Be willing and medically fit to undergo a fresh (newly obtained) diagnostic biopsy of a metastatic lesion or primary site of disease before receiving nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab. "Fresh (newly-obtained)" is defined as a specimen obtained up to 6 weeks prior to initiation of treatment with nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab on Day 1.
7. Fit in either of these categories:

   1. Stage I-III NSCLC patients who develop metastatic disease within 6 months of receiving definitive (curative) treatment that includes platinum-based chemotherapy, and who require biopsy for either confirmation of diagnosis or further molecular or immunohistochemical testing to guide treatment.
   2. Stage IV NSCLC patients with progression of disease following platinum based chemotherapy, and who require biopsy for either confirmation of diagnosis or further molecular or immunohistochemical testing to guide treatment.
   3. Stage IV NSCLC patients who will receive nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab as the standard of care in special circumstances (eg, when chemotherapy is contraindicated or if a patient declines to be treated with chemotherapy).
8. Be willing to undergo at least 4 fine needle aspirations for experimental purposes at the time of the standard of care biopsy.
9. Have a performance status of 0 or 1 on the ECOG Performance Scale.

Exclusion Criteria:

The subject must be excluded from participating in the trial if the subject:

1. Is currently participating in and receiving therapy as part of a different clinical trial.
2. Is not a candidate to receive nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab as determined by the patient's oncologist.
3. Has an active infection requiring systemic therapy.
4. Has a history or current evidence of any condition, therapy, or laboratory abnormality that might; (1) confound the results of the trial, (2) that would substantially increase risk of incurring adverse events (AEs) from nivolumab, pembrolizumab or atezolizumab, (3) that would interfere with the subject's participation for the full duration of the trial, or (4) is not in the best interest of the subject to participate, in the opinion of the treating investigator.
5. Has known psychiatric or substance abuse disorders that would interfere with cooperation with the requirements of the trial.
6. Is pregnant or breastfeeding.

* Adult males or females aged 18 years or over

* ECOG performance status 0 or 1
* Predicted life expectancy of 3 months or more
* Ability to comply with study procedures in the Investigator's opinion
* Recovered to Grade 1 from the effects (excluding alopecia) of any prior therapy for their malignancies Adequate lung function
* Adequate renal function
* Adequate hepatic function
* Adequate bone marrow function
* Adequate coagulation tests: PT and aPTT within normal range or international normalized ratio (INR) ≤1.5
* Meeting reproductive status requirements
* Subjects must provide written informed consent to participate
* Willing to consent to tumour biopsies during the study

Exclusion Criteria:

* Pregnant or breastfeeding females
* Known history or evidence of significant immunodeficiency due to underlying illness
* Splenectomy
* Prior allogeneic or autologous bone marrow or organ transplantation
* Any history of renal disease, renal injury or auto-immune disease.
* History of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, drug induced pneumonitis, evidence of active pneumonia or pneumonitis on computed tomography scan
* Clinically or radiologically suspected, or evidence of, lymphangitic carcinomatosis
* Active infections requiring antibiotics, physician monitoring or recurrent fevers \>100.4˚F (38.0˚C) associated with a clinical diagnosis of active infection
* Active viral disease or positive test for hepatitis B virus using hepatitis B surface antigen test or positive test for hepatitis C virus (HCV) using HCV ribonucleic acid or HCV antibody test indicating acute or chronic infection.
